entries.title: Hempel’s Paradox of the Ravens
entries.scope: Claim-level traceability review of the article and matching dataset entry. Checked Hempel’s 1945 attribution and publication metadata; the equivalence between ‘all ravens are black’ and ‘all non-black things are non-ravens’; the instance-principle/equivalence-condition derivation; Hempel’s qualitative treatment and role of background knowledge; the distinction between qualitative confirmation and Bayesian degrees of support; assumptions underlying a standard Bayesian treatment and Vranas’s published objection; I. J. Good’s counterexample as reported in Sprenger; editorial teaching analogies; and metadata reconciliation. This is an editorial source-traceability status, not a judgment that any account is correct, an exhaustive literature review, or expert review.
entries.summary: The article now explains the paradox as a result within Hempel’s qualitative account, deriving the white-shoe result from the instance principle and equivalence condition rather than presenting a questionable three-principle summary. It distinguishes Hempel’s qualitative result from Bayesian comparisons of degree, specifies that Bayesian results depend on probability and background assumptions, and reports Vranas’s criticism as a challenge to one standard solution. Good’s artificial counterexample is attributed through Sprenger rather than presented as directly consulted primary testimony. The revised Further Reading list distinguishes the primary essay, SEP overview, scholarly manuscript, and a publisher abstract for Vranas. Relevant passages in appropriate primary and scholarly sources were read; whole works and some cited originals were not.

claim_evidence.material_claim: A black raven is an instance of ‘All ravens are black’; its logically equivalent contrapositive is ‘All non-black things are non-ravens’; under Hempel’s instance criterion and equivalence condition, a non-black non-raven such as a white shoe counts as confirming evidence for the raven hypothesis.
claim_evidence.source_title: Studies in the Logic of Confirmation (I.); Confirmation
claim_evidence.exact_location: Hempel, printed pp. 11–13, section 4 and the opening discussion of ‘The “Paradoxes” of Confirmation’; SEP, §1.2, ‘The ravens paradox.’
claim_evidence.finding: The primary passage states the equivalence condition and demonstrates the paradox generated when it is combined with Nicod’s instance criterion. The SEP gives the explicit raven/contrapositive derivation. The article now describes this as Hempel’s qualitative account rather than as a result imposed on every confirmation theory.
claim_evidence.limitation: The sources distinguish logical equivalence from equal degree of support. Hempel’s paper provides a formal account beyond the article’s short pedagogical sketch.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: replaced the inaccurate three-principle summary with the two commitments that generate this derivation and identified the result as account-relative.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Hempel accepts that non-black non-ravens confirm the raven hypothesis in his formal account without additional empirical information, and he explains much of the intuitive resistance by tacit background knowledge.
claim_evidence.source_title: Hempel and the Paradoxes of Confirmation; Confirmation and Induction
claim_evidence.exact_location: Sprenger, §§3–4, printed pp. 14–15, including Hempel’s response as discussed and the background-information diagnosis; IEP §2(a), ‘The Ravens Paradox.’
claim_evidence.finding: The secondary discussions report Hempel’s view that the qualitative confirmation result holds when the evidence is considered without further information; the apparent oddity involves background knowledge such as population proportions or knowing the object is a non-raven. The revised article separates that logical response from whether his formal account adequately handles background information.
claim_evidence.limitation: The account of Hempel’s explanatory response is mediated through scholarly secondary sources; not every detail of his full theory or later revisions was reviewed.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: corrected the conflation of Hempel’s qualitative acceptance with a claim that the support is quantitatively negligible, and stated that background sensitivity remains a limitation.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Some Bayesian treatments distinguish the degree of support from Hempelian qualitative confirmation; conclusions about the comparative or very small support from a white shoe depend on background probabilities and assumptions.

claim_evidence.finding: The sources support distinguishing whether evidence confirms from how strongly it confirms. Bayesian conclusions depend on probability assignments and background conditions; they do not follow from logical equivalence by itself. The article states this without treating one numerical result as settled.

claim_evidence.exact_location: Vranas’s publisher abstract and bibliographic record; Sprenger §5.2, printed pp. 21–22, discussion of Vranas’s objection to the independence assumption.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Good’s examples, as reported by Sprenger, include an artificial probability model in which observing a black raven favors a possibility where the universal hypothesis is false.

claim_evidence.finding: Sprenger describes Good’s two-world construction, specifying 100 black ravens and no white ravens in one world versus 1,000 black ravens and one white raven in the other, with a million other birds in each. entries.title: The Lottery Paradox
entries.scope: Claim-level traceability review of the article and proposed matching data patch. Checked the finite-lottery setup and high-probability inference; the role of threshold-based acceptance, conjunction (agglomeration) closure, and consistency; the distinction between a contradiction believed and jointly inconsistent beliefs; Kyburg's attributed response and other approaches without treating any as a consensus solution; the relation to knowledge; the preface paradox and its Makinson/Wilder attribution; the 1961 bibliographic claim and Wheeler's qualification about an earlier conference formulation and 1963 publication; editorial teaching prompts; and reconciliation of Further Reading URLs and order with the proposed patch. This status records traceability, not the truth or soundness of any philosophical position, an exhaustive literature review, or expert review.
entries.summary: The revised article conditions the lottery inference on a threshold below certainty and conjunction closure, and describes the resulting beliefs as jointly inconsistent rather than automatically saying the agent believes a contradiction. It replaces the unsupported threshold-to-certainty and credence-first/knowledge-first taxonomy with qualified, non-exhaustive response families, and treats the knowledge question as related rather than settled by the paradox. The preface-paradox attribution is tied to Sorensen's SEP discussion of Makinson and Wilder. Wheeler's review supports the 1961 published-account attribution while noting an earlier conference formulation and 1963 publication. The primary book's argument text was not accessible; relevant passages in two SEP entries and Wheeler's scholarly review were read. The article's four Further Reading URLs match the proposed local patch in order; the dataset itself was not modified.

sources.title: Formal Representations of Belief
sources.author: Konstantin Genin and Franz Huber
sources.publication: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Winter 2020 archive; §4.2.2, “The Lockean Threshold,” including the discussion of the Lottery paradox.
sources.access_level: Relevant sections and passages were read in the fixed archived entry; the entire entry was not read.
sources.exact_locations_read: §4.2.2 defines strong and weak Lockean thresholds; the paragraph beginning “The strong Lockean thesis gives rise to the well-known Lottery paradox” sets out a fair N-ticket lottery, the threshold-dependent inference to each ticket's loss, conjunction closure, and the conflict with the belief that some ticket wins. The following paragraphs describe Kyburg's response, authors who reject the strong Lockean thesis, and proposals that add defeating conditions. A later passage on odds-threshold acceptance explains one alternative formal strategy.
sources.limitations: Secondary synthesis, not the primary Kyburg text. It presents a number of formal approaches but does not settle the philosophical dispute or establish that its treatment is exhaustive. The article's use of an illustrative, very large lottery is not asserted as Kyburg's exact original ticket count.

sources.title: Epistemic Paradoxes
sources.author: Roy Sorensen
sources.publication: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Fall 2024 archive; §§3, “Lotteries and the Lottery Paradox,” and 4, “Preface Paradox.”
sources.access_level: Relevant sections and passages were read in the fixed archived entry; the entire entry was not read.
sources.exact_locations_read: §3 states the agglomeration principle, works through a 100-ticket threshold example, explains the route to contradiction, and distinguishes rejecting agglomeration from rejecting sub-certain acceptance rules; it explicitly characterizes Kyburg's response as permitting joint inconsistency without belief in a necessarily false proposition. §4 recounts Wilder's preface, attributes the paradox formulation to D. C. Makinson (1965), states that the preface paradox does not rely on a probabilistic acceptance rule, and discusses its relation to Kyburg's response. The bibliography entry gives Makinson's 1965 publication details.
sources.limitations: A later scholarly account, not direct consultation of Makinson's or Wilder's original texts. The summary's interpretation of the relation between the paradoxes is attributed to Sorensen rather than presented as the only analysis.

claim_evidence.material_claim: In a fair finite lottery with exactly one winner, each individual ticket-loss proposition can be assigned a probability above any fixed threshold below certainty by making the number of tickets large enough; under a simple Lockean rule, each such proposition then qualifies for full belief.
claim_evidence.source_title: Formal Representations of Belief; Epistemic Paradoxes; A Review of the Lottery Paradox
claim_evidence.exact_location: Genin and Huber, §4.2.2, paragraph beginning “The strong Lockean thesis gives rise to the well-known Lottery paradox”; Sorensen, §3, 100-ticket and .99 example; Wheeler, printed p. 1, fair 1,000-ticket and .99 example.
claim_evidence.finding: The sources support the standard threshold setup. The revised article states the generalized finite-N form rather than implying that every merely high probability warrants belief in every theory.
claim_evidence.limitation: The probability inference presupposes a fair lottery with exactly one winner and a specified full-belief threshold rule; the ticket count is illustrative, not asserted to reproduce Kyburg's exact wording.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: replaced the unqualified claim that it simply seems rational to believe each ticket will lose with an explicit conditional on a fixed sub-certain probability threshold.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Combining threshold-licensed beliefs in every ticket's loss with conjunction closure and belief that exactly one ticket wins generates a conflict; rational beliefs may be jointly inconsistent without the agent thereby believing an explicit contradiction, depending on which principles are retained.
claim_evidence.source_title: Epistemic Paradoxes; Formal Representations of Belief; A Review of the Lottery Paradox
claim_evidence.exact_location: Sorensen, §3, numbered agglomeration derivation and paragraph distinguishing belief in a contradiction from joint inconsistency; Genin and Huber, §4.2.2, threshold/conjunction paragraph; Wheeler, printed pp. 1–2, setup and §1.
claim_evidence.finding: The sources establish the tension and show that the exact conclusion depends on the principles being combined. The article now says the beliefs are jointly inconsistent and avoids saying that the agent automatically believes a contradiction.
claim_evidence.limitation: The argument is a formal/philosophical pressure on a package of norms, not a proof that one particular norm must be rejected in all accounts of belief.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: explicitly named probability, conjunction closure, and consistency as the tension; corrected “led to believe a contradiction” to “beliefs are jointly inconsistent.”

claim_evidence.material_claim: Kyburg is associated with rejecting conjunction closure, while other approaches reject or qualify a simple high-probability-to-full-belief rule; the article should not present one response or taxonomy as standard or settled.
claim_evidence.source_title: Formal Representations of Belief; Epistemic Paradoxes; A Review of the Lottery Paradox
claim_evidence.exact_location: Genin and Huber, §4.2.2, paragraphs on Kyburg's response, those who find the strong Lockean thesis untenable, and proposals adding defeating conditions; Sorensen, §3, dilemma and characterization of Kyburg; Wheeler, printed pp. 1–2, §1, discussion of disagreement about rational acceptance and competing diagnoses.
claim_evidence.finding: The sources document distinct responses and continuing disagreement. The revised article gives examples as non-exhaustive families and does not call any one solution standard.
claim_evidence.limitation: The sources reviewed are not an exhaustive survey of every contemporary response; the article's “no single agreed resolution” is limited to the fact that the consulted accounts describe distinct positions and diagnoses.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: removed the unsupported threshold-to-certainty/credence-first/knowledge-first list and replaced it with a cautious, non-exhaustive summary grounded in the SEP and Wheeler.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The lottery paradox raises a related question about whether statistical evidence can support knowledge, but the argument itself does not settle that question or establish that probabilistic reasoning generally is unreliable.
claim_evidence.source_title: A Review of the Lottery Paradox; Epistemic Paradoxes
claim_evidence.exact_location: Wheeler, printed p. 19, §3.1, discussion distinguishing statistical evidence as a basis for rational belief from its sufficiency for knowledge and presenting Dana Nelkin's contrary view; Sorensen, §3, explanation of the lottery argument and its assumptions.
claim_evidence.finding: Wheeler explicitly distinguishes the knowledge question from rational belief and presents disagreement about statistical evidence. The article now marks knowledge as a related debate rather than an inference established by the paradox.
claim_evidence.limitation: Wheeler's account is one analysis of a contested issue; no psychological survey supports a claim about what “most people feel,” so that claim was removed.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: removed the generalization about what most people feel and the inference that the scenario by itself shows knowledge requires more than high probability.

claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: retained the attribution but made its evidential basis explicit and described the preface case as distinct from the lottery argument.

entries.title: Norman the Clairvoyant
entries.scope: Claim-level traceability review of the article and matching dataset entry. Checked BonJour attribution and publication metadata; the Norman Case IV setup; BonJour's argument and its framing as an objection to simple process reliabilism and broader externalist accounts; the distinction between simple process reliabilism and several later responses; qualifications about internalism, externalism, knowledge and justification; the Gettier comparison; the Mr. Truetemp relationship; explicitly editorial teaching framing; and article/dataset metadata reconciliation. This status records traceability of the revised article, not the truth or success of BonJour's argument, a consensus view, an exhaustive survey of reliabilist theories, or expert review.
entries.summary: The revised article preserves BonJour's stipulated Norman scenario and his perspective-based objection, but no longer presents the case as automatically decisive against every reliabilist or externalist theory. It distinguishes the challenge to the sufficiency of simple process reliability from different published replies, qualifies the internalism/externalism framing, and identifies Mr. Truetemp and the thermometer comparison as related-but-distinct case and editorial analogy. Relevant passages in BonJour's primary text, two SEP entries, the IEP reliabilism entry, and the SEP knowledge-analysis entry were read. The publisher's record verifies the article's publication details. The proposed data patch's five reference URLs and their order match the revised Further Reading section exactly; the dataset date is updated to 2026-11-01.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Norman has, under normally obtaining conditions, a completely reliable clairvoyant faculty for certain subject matters; he has no reasons or evidence for or against the power or his possession of it; he forms a true belief that the President is in New York City through that faculty.
claim_evidence.source_title: Externalist Theories of Empirical Knowledge
claim_evidence.exact_location: Case IV, printed p. 62; corroborated by Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Reliabilist Epistemology,” §2.1.
claim_evidence.finding: The revised scenario closely tracks BonJour's stipulated Case IV and does not treat clairvoyance as an actual-world claim.
claim_evidence.limitation: This is a hypothetical stipulation in a philosophical argument, not testimony that clairvoyance exists.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: retained the case's key assumptions, and clarified that the scenario is stipulated rather than asserted as fact.

claim_evidence.material_claim: BonJour argues that Norman's belief is epistemically irrational or unjustified from Norman's own perspective, despite the stipulated truth and reliability.
claim_evidence.source_title: Externalist Theories of Empirical Knowledge
claim_evidence.exact_location: Printed pp. 62–64, especially BonJour's argument that Norman lacks a reason to treat the belief as having a reliable source and is epistemically irresponsible; see also pp. 65–67 for the broader argumentative framing and possible replies.
claim_evidence.finding: The primary text supports the attribution to BonJour. The revised article marks this as BonJour's argument and uses perspective-based framing, rather than reporting it as a settled verdict.
claim_evidence.limitation: A primary philosophical argument establishes what BonJour argues, not that his conclusion is correct. The scanned PDF text has OCR artifacts.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: attributed the irrationality/irresponsibility judgment to BonJour and identified the conclusion as his argument.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Norman is used to challenge the sufficiency of simple process reliability for justification, but the case does not automatically refute every theory that gives reliability a role.
claim_evidence.source_title: Reliabilist Epistemology; Internalist vs. Externalist Conceptions of Epistemic Justification
claim_evidence.exact_location: Reliabilist Epistemology §2.1 frames Norman as the clairvoyance problem for process reliabilism and presents different responses; Internalist vs. Externalist Conceptions §§1 and 2.1 distinguishes justification and knowledge debates and states that BonJour's intuitions challenge pure externalism, not a wide range of possible externalist views.
claim_evidence.finding: The two reference works support distinguishing the standard process-reliabilist challenge from a blanket conclusion about all reliabilist or externalist theories. BonJour's own paper frames his conclusion more broadly as a challenge to externalist justification; the revised article notes this broader original framing separately.
claim_evidence.limitation: These are secondary syntheses and do not resolve whether a particular reliabilist variant succeeds.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: narrowed the article's claim about the case's reach and retained a sentence describing BonJour's broader original challenge.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The article defines the simple process-reliabilist target as the claim that a belief is justified when produced by a sufficiently reliable process.
claim_evidence.source_title: Reliabilist Epistemology
claim_evidence.exact_location: §1.2 on process reliability and justification, and §2.1 on the clairvoyance problem.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP discussion supports the simplified characterization as pedagogical shorthand for the simple process-reliabilist claim at issue.
claim_evidence.limitation: The article presents a concise teaching formulation, not a complete formal definition of every process-reliabilist theory.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: expressly labels the account 'simple process reliabilism' and avoids generalizing it to every reliabilist view.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Published responses to Norman differ: some defend an externalist verdict, some deny that their theory entails justification in the case, and some introduce additional conditions; examples include approved-list, primal-system, and evidentialist–reliabilist approaches.
claim_evidence.source_title: Reliabilist Epistemology; Internalist vs. Externalist Conceptions of Epistemic Justification; Reliabilism
claim_evidence.exact_location: Reliabilist Epistemology §2.1 (approved-list reliabilism and primal systems), §4.2 (evidentialist–reliabilist hybrids); Internalist vs. Externalist Conceptions §2.1 (defend Norman's justification, deny entailment, or combine internal/external conditions); IEP Reliabilism §3(a) (Goldman's and other approaches).
claim_evidence.finding: The sources support presenting the replies as distinct strategies rather than as a single reliabilist answer. The revised article uses illustrative categories and does not claim the list is exhaustive.
claim_evidence.limitation: The SEP and IEP sections survey selected responses; no exhaustive review of the literature or adjudication of each proposal was undertaken.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: replaced the compressed 'reliabilists reply' account with a non-exhaustive, differentiated summary.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Internalism/externalism is a broad framing, with differing conceptions of accessibility and external dependence; some views combine internal and external conditions, and philosophers disagree about whether justification/rationality is required for knowledge.
claim_evidence.source_title: Internalist vs. Externalist Conceptions of Epistemic Justification
claim_evidence.exact_location: §1 on internal/external and justification/knowledge distinctions; §2.1 on mixed internal and external conditions and lack of consensus about knowledge requiring rational belief or justification.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP passage directly supports the qualifications added to the article's binary framing.
claim_evidence.limitation: The entry is a scholarly overview; the article's one-paragraph summary cannot represent the full range of positions.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: identified accessibilism specifically, acknowledged mixed theories, and stated that the justification/knowledge relationship is disputed.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The Norman case differs from standard Gettier cases: Gettier cases are commonly presented as justified true beliefs that still appear not to be knowledge due to epistemic luck, whereas Norman challenges whether his belief is justified given lack of reason to trust its source.
claim_evidence.source_title: The Analysis of Knowledge; Externalist Theories of Empirical Knowledge
claim_evidence.exact_location: SEP The Analysis of Knowledge §3 on Gettier cases, justified true belief and epistemic luck; BonJour, Case IV, pp. 62–64, on the Norman justification objection.
claim_evidence.finding: The comparison is supported as a contrast between the standard focus of Gettier cases and BonJour's stated Norman objection. The revised article expressly presents it as a teaching contrast and allows that related questions about knowledge may arise.
claim_evidence.limitation: The contrast is a simplification for readers; the article does not claim that all Gettier cases share one precise diagnosis or that the problems are unrelated.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: qualified the contrast and labeled it as teaching framing.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Lehrer's Mr. Truetemp is a related but distinct example in which reliable temperature beliefs arise from an implanted thermometer-like device without the subject's knowledge of that source.
claim_evidence.source_title: Reliabilism
claim_evidence.exact_location: IEP §3(a), account of Mr. Truetemp and the tempucomp, alongside the Norman discussion; the entry attributes the example to Keith Lehrer (1990).
claim_evidence.finding: The entry describes the distinct device-and-temperature setup and explicitly calls it a similar case. The article now preserves that relationship without equating the cases.
claim_evidence.limitation: Lehrer's original book was not accessed; the attribution and scenario detail are supported here by a scholarly reference-work account.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: described Truetemp as related but distinct and noted that the original case differs in its details.
